title: Ten minutes of compassion
hookLine: put the compassion research into one sit

lines: AN OLD ORDER, A SHORT LINE.
cards: You can't sit with a finding on a Tuesday night. For a stretch of days, this path has piled them up. Feeling another's pain can swamp you; warmth and a wish to help hold up better.
Carers wear out. The skill can be trained, it can widen to people unlike you, and it has to include the person doing it. Today the whole pile goes into one practice.
An old one already exists for exactly this, with a set order of people and a short line to say to each.

teach.h: THE MOTHER AND HER ONLY CHILD.
teach.b: First, the picture, back from the day on bias. The short discourse on loving-kindness in the Sutta Nipata aims at one image: a mother guarding her only child, held as a boundless heart toward every living being.

The Pali word is metta, usually translated loving-kindness. Second, the order. A Theravada manual called the Path of Purification, which tradition credits to the commentator Buddhaghosa, lays out the whole route.
Yesterday it supplied the starting point: yourself.
Then someone dear. Then someone neutral, a face you pass without a thought. Then someone hostile.
The aim, the manual says, is to break down the barriers between these people until the wish is the same for each. Third, what the research adds.

The studies this path looked at suggest that feeling another's pain can drown you, while warmth and a wish to help hold up better. These phrases don't ask you to feel anyone's pain. They ask you to wish them well.
And starting with yourself is yesterday's line, me too, built into the method.
Fourth, when it sticks. Nothing has to be felt on cue. The manual expects resistance, especially at the hostile person, and advises going back to an easier person for a while, then returning.
Teachers word the phrases differently; common ones are plain: may you be well, may you be safe, may you be at ease. And the ten minutes? Five stops, two minutes each.

how: In loving-kindness practice, Buddhists and others silently repeat short wishes such as "may you be well," moving from themselves to a dear person, a neutral person, a difficult person and finally all beings.

games.q: what does “ten minutes of compassion” mean?
o: a loving-kindness sit in order: you, dear, neutral, hard, then all
a short daily break from caring for other people
ten minutes of feeling another person's pain as your own

games.q: ten minutes of compassion: tap the pairs.
p: a mother guarding her only child
go back to an easier person

s: the phrases are one fixed wording that every teacher uses
teachers word them differently. common ones are plain: may you be well, may you be safe, may you be at ease.
the phrases ask you to feel the other person's pain
they ask you to wish them well, which is the warmth the research found holds up better than drowning in someone's pain.
the manual expects resistance and suggests going back to an easier person
nothing has to be felt on cue. you return to the hard person later.

games.q: you reach the hostile person in the sequence and your chest tightens. what do you do?
o: push through and force the wish out.
go back to an easier person for a while, then return.
games.why: the Path of Purification expects this. it advises going back to the earlier, easier people for a while, and then turning to the hard one again.

practice: One quick pass through all five stops.

Silently, to yourself first: may I be well, may I be safe, may I be at ease; then to someone dear; then a neutral face, a cashier or a neighbor whose name you never learned; then, only if it feels possible, someone difficult, and if not, stay a little longer with the neutral face; last, everyone at once.
If you pray, you can hold these same people in your own prayer instead.

wordCard.voice: Ten minutes of compassion. Loving-kindness in the old manual's order: you, someone dear, someone neutral, someone hard, then everyone. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali, from the Buddhist texts: loving-kindness, the warm wish for another's well-being.

carryVoice: Your line: may you be well. The full ten minutes is two for each of the five, whenever you have them. See you tomorrow.
